drafts.draft: A useful first distinction is when resistance starts: before entering, at lights-out, when the parent leaves, or after a later waking. Those moments point to different barriers. I would avoid changing the whole room at once; observe one moment, choose one small experiment, and keep the response consistent for several nights.

A child can enjoy a room during the day and still resist sleeping there. That often means the barrier is not the decoration itself. Check whether the difficult moment is entering, lights-out, separation, or a night waking. Change one variable only so you can tell what actually helped.
儿童房已经布置好了，孩子为什么还是不肯自己睡？先别继续加东西。观察抗拒从什么时候开始：进房前、关灯时、父母离开时，还是半夜醒来后。一次只改一个变量，才知道真正的阻力在哪里。
Your child may not fear the room. They may fear the exact moment the light changes—or the moment you leave. Before adding more lights, ask: when does the resistance begin? One answer. One experiment.

drafts.draft: When a child starts in their own bed but returns later, note the time, whether they are fully awake, and what they ask for. This can be a different problem from refusing the room at bedtime. A small, predictable response is easier to evaluate than changing the room and routine together.
